strategic_notes.text: The creator returns during the offseason to discuss two Einstein matches. He introduces 2481 as a tall, high-capacity dumper that wants a large neutral-zone collection followed by two substantial discharges per shift. He immediately pairs that scoring potential with crossing limitations and the maneuvering demands of a rectangular robot. The first example is Curie’s 8613, 6800 and 254 against Milstein’s 4915, 2481 and 1678. The second compares Milstein with Johnson’s 6324, 4946 and 2337.

Keep archetype and role separate. A high-capacity robot may be its alliance’s main scorer, but how it is supplied and escorted determines whether capacity becomes scored fuel. Do not extract “tall dumper is bad” from a source that repeatedly praises its output and shows several close contests. This is an outcome-aware retrospective: its explanation of why a plan worked is useful evidence of the creator’s theory, but cannot establish what the teams intended at the time or what an early-season design team could confidently predict.

The account describes 6800 taking a deep collection arc, 254 contesting 1678, and 8613 meeting 2481 so 2481 cannot reach the desired fuel. It separately reports 4915 getting jammed on its own trench, leaving a planned collection area untouched. The creator assumes Curie specifically prepared the autonomous interaction against 2481, but offers no team statement. In his account, Milstein loses the autonomous advantage on which its tall-dumper plan usually relies.

Three mechanisms of reduced output must remain distinct: fuel taken first by an opponent, movement constrained by another robot and a partner failing to execute its own route. The official auto fuel, Curie 188 versus Milstein 118, confirms an alliance difference; it cannot allocate the 70-fuel margin to those causes. To audit the anti-auto claim, align actual starting poses and compare earlier routes before and after the alleged change. The source’s confidence about prescouting is a hypothesis. A fast deep sweep also requires loaded exit clearance, not just reaching the pile first.

The creator praises Milstein for using the transition to fill rather than immediately mirror scoring. He says 1678 opens its hopper into a configuration that relies on the bump, using the briefly uncontested middle to collect more. However, 2481 is delayed filling after Curie’s earlier collection and is still in a vulnerable approach when Curie returns. The commentary describes Curie collecting and passing the middle while making 2481 and 1678’s return difficult, reducing their useful active cycles.

The relevant state is not simply “can use the trench” on a specification sheet. It is whether the currently expanded, loaded robot can use it during the next escape. Larger storage changes both potential discharge and the route set. Staying to fill the last portion of a hopper can be costly if the defender reaches the crossing first; leaving partially full can preserve more active scoring time. This is a conditional scheduling trade, not an instruction to abandon capacity. Record fill level as unknown unless it is counted, and compare expected additional fuel with the distribution of return delays under the actual defense.

As Curie scores its prepared fuel, the creator describes 1678 stealing rather than competing with 2481 for the remaining neutral-zone supply. He argues a trench-capable configuration makes that assignment less vulnerable to 8613 denying a bump crossing. He also describes 4915 functioning as a turret cleanup passer. He briefly judges Milstein’s prepared field state potentially competitive because fuel is held in hoppers and corners, then describes 254 slipping past an attempted interception to remove a prepared corner pile.

A fuel map should include prepared reserves, robot inventory and which robot can legally and physically reach each reserve. A pile’s value is conditional on the route to it surviving the opponent’s next action. This is why a snapshot of potential points is not a score forecast. The creator’s approximate hundreds of waiting points are not an independently counted inventory. A mobility advantage can make the same robot the preferred thief in one configuration and a poor thief when its hopper is extended, so retrieval must include configuration and match phase rather than attach one permanent stealing role to a team number.

The source describes 254 and 6800 stealing from different sides, then resuming pressure on Milstein’s neutral-zone returns. Later, 2481 goes deep to steal. The commentator disagrees with giving that job to a bump-only robot when 1678 is available, while admitting he does not know the team’s reason. He says 254 suspends a scoring cycle long enough to slow 2481’s exit and allow 8613 to arrive. He cannot determine whether the resulting apparent hold is a pin because the camera does not show the necessary contact clearly.

This is a relay between a scorer and defender: the scorer need not hold an opponent indefinitely if a brief delay lets a better-positioned partner take over. The cost is the scorer’s immediate lost output; the possible benefit is denying a much longer opponent return and freeing the scorer afterward. Neither is quantified here. The source’s uncertainty about pinning is essential evidence, not a caveat to strip off. Even a complete broadcast review may leave the contact occluded; another angle or the official foul record may be needed, and absence of a call is not a general interpretation of the rule.

The creator describes 254 exploiting time bought by the delay to clean the neutral zone, 8613 continuing to interfere and 6800’s position or passing action forcing 2481 toward another bump. He is unsure whether that particular 6800 action is intentional and guesses 8613 may be losing battery performance. The conclusion praises Curie’s coordination while observing that Milstein’s fuel scoring stays competitive despite the disruption. The source’s spoken figures are not a per-robot scoring breakdown.

The official final is Curie 717–632, with auto fuel 188–118 and subsequent fuel 529–509. Those latter values are alliance totals after auto; they must not become “2481 scored 509” or “one robot was only 20 behind.” The 20-fuel post-auto difference coexists with a 70-fuel autonomous difference. The game can reward a high-capacity architecture even in a match where an opponent exploits its routes. This is precisely why a design recommendation needs a partner plan and an anti-defense validation, rather than replacing one celebrated mechanism with another based solely on which alliance won this example.

strategic_notes.text: In Milstein–Johnson, the creator describes 2481 receiving a less-contested deep collection, 4915 completing its auto and 1678 cutting ahead of 2337 and toward 4946. He speculates about prescouting rather than claiming team confirmation. Milstein wins autonomous by nine fuel. The creator then introduces his thesis that losing autonomous by a very small margin may be advantageous because of the sequence of active shifts and who can control the next returned fuel.

The nine-fuel difference is a measured alliance result, while “lose by one” is a strategic hypothesis. Do not convert a conditional argument into an instruction to throw away autonomous points or deliberately accept route failures. The hypothesis depends on the cost of the lost auto margin, expected transition production, who controls the middle when fuel returns, the ability to store supply and whether the opponent can interrupt the setup. Another alliance can win auto and still control those same states, as the Daly series account illustrates. An evaluation needs matched scenarios or a validated model rather than a win-loss anecdote.

The account describes Johnson sending 6324 to score an already loaded hopper, using 2337 for some scoring and later support, and keeping 4946 in a cleanup/passing role. The creator likes having at least one capable neutral-zone cleanup robot, while wondering whether 2337 could have spent more of the transition denying 2481. He later praises 2337 for switching among defense, a screen and small scoring contributions, rather than staying in one fixed task all match.

The opportunity cost of transition collection depends on starting inventory. A loaded robot gains less from another collection pass and can cash in the brief scoring window; a suitable partner can still secure supply. The source therefore offers a hybrid alternative to both “everyone score now” and “everyone collect now.” It does not prove every alliance needs exactly one dedicated passer. A third robot can contribute by changing another robot’s accessible path or timing, and that effect should be evaluated alongside its own points. Visual auditing should record the order of those job changes rather than infer it from a season-average statistic.

The creator pauses the match to discuss 4946’s rounded or semicircular bumper area. He argues it can rotate and roll around contact that would hold a flat-sided square, and distinguishes a continuous curve from a hexagon or octagon with flat faces. He also explains that a defender obstructed by 6324’s pick temporarily faces an offensive problem: it must escape the screening robot before reaching its original target. His square-on-square defense model emphasizes keeping contact faces aligned, using rotation and not overcommitting to a translational feint.

This is an interesting mechanical hypothesis because the perimeter changes contact geometry and the moment generated by a push. It is not a proof that a rounded robot always has leverage or that polygons are always trapped. Real contact includes compliant bumpers, friction, traction limits, module directions, loaded inertia and nearby walls. A curved perimeter can also change packaging, bumper construction and available acquisition width. The transfer test should compare the complete loaded drivetrains and controlled contact angles. The pick reversal is a driver-training insight: a good defender needs escape practice as well as pursuit practice. Team intent and the exact curvature remain unverified without primary geometry and footage.

The commentary describes 1678 attempting a steal while its hopper is extended, making it bump-only at that instant. 6324 notices and interrupts the return rather than continuing to fill itself. The creator estimates 6324 has a much smaller load and 1678 a larger one; he says the delay consumes roughly the remaining useful scoring interval. He also acknowledges that 1678 still removes fuel from Johnson and could pass or score it later, so the steal is not automatically valueless.

Value the inventories on a schedule. Removing fifty hypothetical fuel from an opponent is not the same as adding fifty score now, and a delayed load can become exposed to a reciprocal steal. Likewise, a small hopper on a support robot is not automatically a reason to defend: the partner needs a current scoring window worth protecting, and the delay must survive the opponent’s available escape. The exact hopper counts and twelve-second estimate are not independently measured. A visual event log should mark the route block, changed configuration, attempted escapes, release and actual first scoring time, with unknown counts left null.

The creator describes 6324 screening to let 4946 leave while 1678 and 2481 collide or congest the middle. He then notes 6324 taking back fuel from Milstein’s side during part of its own scoring time. His explanation is that the neutral zone has become sparse partly because so much fuel is already held in 1678 and 2481. The initial Milstein steal has value, but the delayed use of that inventory allows Johnson to recover some of the supposed advantage.

An alliance can be rich in fuel but poor in immediately accessible scoring opportunities. Large loaded hoppers reduce shared field supply for everybody, including the owner’s partners; an opponent with another reachable reserve may temporarily have the better play. This is a dynamic inventory and timing problem, not simply hopper capacity times shooter rate. The collision and screening intent still require footage. A useful agent should be able to explain why the same 6324 can screen, steal and score at different moments without collapsing those actions into a generic “support” paragraph or assuming every action was a preplanned call.

The source closes by following Johnson’s prepared corner fuel and loaded robots, Milstein’s late effort to find reserves and both Milstein scorers returning for final cycles. He interprets the remaining supply and shift order as the reason Johnson can win despite losing auto narrowly. He also gives a no-penalty comparison of 678–691. The final recorded match is 688–691 because Milstein receives ten penalty points. The commentary’s claim that the auto loser has the better teleop conditions is an interpretation of this match state.

Preserve both margins: three in the official final, thirteen in fuel or clean output, with the penalty difference identified. This close result is sensitive to many events besides active-shift order. Compare it to the upper-bracket Daly example: there, winning auto accompanies strong transition position and cleanup that deny the opponent an easy supply setup. Here, the source argues the auto winner does not maintain that control and also faces crossing and screening problems. The transferable principle is to model the next supply state and routes under either autonomous outcome. It is not that auto has negative value, and the source does not establish a universal optimal margin.

The introduction treats the upper-bracket meeting plus three finals as one strategic series. Daly fields 4065, 4414 and 1323; Newton fields 868, 2046 and 2910. The creator credits both Daly’s scoring pair and 4065’s defense. Later passages explicitly describe interruptions to 1323, 868 and 2046. The account therefore contains several changing robot-availability states rather than four repetitions of the same six healthy machines.

An architecture comparison should condition on operational state. A two-turret alliance beating two dumpers in the final result does not establish an unconditional turret advantage: starting positions, autonomous contact, defensive assignments, fuel distribution and failures all change between matches. Conversely, describing the series only as breakdowns discards the account of deliberate supply control. Preserve both explanations until footage and team logs can separate them. The six active robots are the match-specific roster; a reserve on the championship alliance must not be silently treated as an active participant in these four recordings.

The creator describes 1323 beginning at an angle and cutting ahead of 2910 rather than first translating sideways. He says this leaves one corner of fuel but permits a larger sweep around the pile. He attributes 2910’s later misalignment and intake corner catching to the rotation caused by that encounter. On the other side, 4414 makes a central pass with a following 4065 route, collects near the hub wall and returns to score from the outpost side. He connects 4414’s net and hopper to retaining a large collection across the bump and clearing it before autonomous ends. His belief that the teams timed the opposing routes is explicitly an assumption.

The useful design requirement is an autonomous system whose acquisition envelope, collision recovery and route compatibility are evaluated together. A route can abandon a small pocket yet improve total possession by reaching a more valuable arc first. A high collection rate can create an exit-path problem if the loaded robot cannot traverse the selected obstacle without shedding fuel. A net is therefore part of the mobility–storage interface, not an isolated capacity feature. None of this gives a dimension, actual retained count or certified causal diagnosis of 2910’s auto error. Reproduce the route interaction with synchronized overhead video and logs before concluding that the same cut always defeats the same opponent.

The account praises 4065 for ending near midfield and immediately reaching across to contest Newton’s transition fuel. It contrasts 868 ending deeper on its own side and arriving after 1323 and 4414 have already collected and moved ahead of it. The commentator argues that a defender arriving late misses a short opportunity to reduce the autonomous winner’s transition scoring. He describes Daly converting its uncontested collection into sustained transition output.

Treat autonomous terminal pose as the initial condition of teleop, including the defender. Maximizing a small autonomous contribution may be a poor trade if it places that robot too far from the next high-value interception. The source describes a timing window, not a universal instruction to send a defender immediately across the field. The outcome depends on the actual active-hub schedule, legal routes, expected collector arrival and whether intercepting one scorer leaves a partner free. Official fuel confirms a 65–30 transition advantage for Daly in this match, but that alliance total cannot measure the individual value of 4065’s terminal pose or prove the stated cause.

The creator describes 1323 and 4414 splitting the neutral zone, circling through fuel and passing it back while their hub is inactive. They also occupy enough of 2046’s path to make acquisition awkward. He contrasts this with a dumper stopping to pass a batch. In his account, 2046 finds little fuel in the neutral zone, returns toward its own corner reserves and later has difficulty obtaining another hopper. He mentions 868 holding fuel and a 4065 blocker delaying part of 2910’s final discharge.

This is a coupled acquisition, passing and interference role. Passing while moving can let an off-shift robot keep collecting instead of serializing collect, stop, orient and release; the same motion can close an opponent’s useful approach. That does not make every turret a good moving passer. Intake throughput, feed continuity, aiming under motion, range, loaded acceleration and the ability to keep fuel on the intended side all matter. Fuel temporarily held in a third robot is another supply state, even if that robot scores little. The source supplies neither a complete fuel ledger nor timing measurements, so avoid turning this account into a quantified claim that turrets always clean the field faster than drums.

The analysis follows 2046 from an unproductive neutral-zone visit into a corner collection, then into a later cross-field steal. It says the later departure gives 1323 roughly three additional seconds before the steal arrives. In the other direction, 4414 can leave earlier to remove Newton’s stashed fuel. Later, 1323 screens 868 so 4414 can cross back, while 2046 again arrives late. The creator frames these actions as compounding consequences of the earlier neutral-zone cleanup, not independent isolated tricks.

Supply denial may first force a detour, then postpone a steal, then expose a partner’s prepared pile; simply counting immediate defended scoring seconds misses those downstream opportunities. His explanation is that the dual turrets can continue hunting scattered fuel while moving, whereas the dumper pair loses efficiency when it can no longer fill efficiently before returning to a firing position.

A hopper-full shooter rate is not the marginal match rate when the remaining fuel is dispersed. Distinguish release-limited, collection-limited and route-limited phases.
